problem_motivation.content: There is no satisfactory microscopic theory for the reported anomalous phenomena in hydride metals.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: A satisfactory microscopic theory of such phenomena is still lacking.

problem_motivation.content: The spectrum and transition probabilities of excited coherent states remain an open problem.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: These issues require knowledge of the spectrum and transition probabilities of the excited coherent states, which remains one of the main open problems of the model.

problem_motivation.content: A complete theory is still needed that combines microscopic coherent-ground-state derivation, localized proton spectrum, and many-body excited-state and weak-matrix-element calculations.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: A complete theory of coher- ent electron capture should therefore combine the microscopic derivation of the coherent ground state, the localized proton spectrum of Ref. [3], and a many-body calculation of the excited coherent states and of their weak-interaction matrix elements.

problem_motivation.content: The key unresolved issue is the structure of excited coherent states
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The central open problem is the structure of the excited coherent states.

problem_motivation.content: Electron capture needs excited coherent states with proper energies and strengths, not just a stable ground state
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, electron capture requires not only a stable coherent ground state, but also excited coherent states with suitable transition energies and transition strengths.

problem_motivation.content: A fuller theory should derive the excited spectrum microscopically from the proton-photon Hamiltonian
problem_motivation.evidence_span: but a more complete theory should derive the 10 excited spectrum from the microscopic proton–photon Hamiltonian.

problem_motivation.content: The key physical challenge is coherent energy conversion across strongly mismatched energy scales
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The relevant physical problem is therefore a form of coherent energy conversion between strongly mismatched energy scales.

problem_motivation.content: What must ultimately be computed is the spectral weight coupling the weak operator to neutron-plus-neutrino final states, not just total stored energy
problem_motivation.evidence_span: the ultimate quantity to be computed is not only the total energy stored in a coherence domain, but the spectral weight with which the local weak operator couples the initial coherent state to final states containing a neutron and a neutrino.

problem_motivation.content: It remains open whether the response has a coherent contribution scaling super-extensively with proton number
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Establishing whether such a response contains a coherent contribution scaling super-extensively with the number of participating protons remains an open problem.

prior_approach.content: Previous studies examined formation of the coherent ground state in a model of many protons oscillating at interstitial lattice sites and coupled to confined electromagnetic modes.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The formation of the coherent ground state has been studied in Refs. [1, 2]. In that model, a large number N of protons are bound to interstitial sites of a cubic lattice and oscillate with a local frequency determined by the electrostatic potential of the site. The protons are also coupled to electromagnetic modes confined inside a finite region of the material.

prior_approach.content: Prior work studied formation of the coherent ground state.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The formation of the coherent ground state has been studied in Refs. [1, 2].

prior_approach.content: A recent simplified-model study provided numerical evidence for coherent-state-mediated high-frequency transfer.
prior_approach.evidence_span: More recently, Ref. [14] has provided numerical evidence, in a simplified model of coherent harmonic qubits, that high-frequency energy transfer between external oscillators can occur only when the intermediate low-frequency oscillators are in a coherent state.

prior_approach.content: Widom and Larsen previously suggested electron capture in condensed matter.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The occurrence of EC in condensed matter has been previously suggested by Widom and Larsen [4].

prior_approach.content: They hypothesized that missing electron-capture energy comes from an increased effective electron mass due to electromagnetic interactions in matter.
prior_approach.evidence_span: the missing energy in case of initial particles at rest was hypothesized to come from the increase of the effective electron mass due to the electromagnetic electron interaction in matter.

prior_approach.content: Widom and Larsen also proposed a gamma-ray suppression mechanism based on the heavy-electron hypothesis.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Widom and Larsen defended their proposal also in other articles [19– 21] and described a possible suppression mechanism of the gamma rays which originate from transmutations of heavy elements and reactions such as p+n →D+γ and D+n → T +γ. This suppression mechanism is also based on the heavy-electron hypothesis.

prior_approach.content: Gamberale previously analyzed electron capture by coherent protons.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The electron capture by coherent protons as proposed in this paper has been previ- ously analyzed by Gamberale [30].

prior_approach.content: That work estimated neutron production rates once a coherent excitation above threshold is available.
prior_approach.evidence_span: This made it possible to address a question which is not treated in the present review of the coherence mechanism itself, namely the or- der of magnitude of the neutron production rate once a coherent excitation above the electron-capture threshold is available.

prior_approach.content: That work also included rate equations connecting pumping to final energy output.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The work also includes rate equations relating the pumping process to the final energy output, which are clearly relevant to applications.

prior_approach.content: Ref. [30] modeled the coherent ground state with a collective mixing-angle parametrization fixed by energy minimization, and represented excited states as nearby states with slightly changed collective parameters.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The coherent ground state is parametrized by a collective mixing angle, fixed by minimization of the energy. A coherent excited state is then represented by a nearby state in the same class, with slightly different values of the collective parameters, for example a modified mixing angle and a modified collective momentum.

prior_approach.content: The electron-capture final state in the prior treatment was constructed by applying destruction operators to the many-body coherent state, removing one proton and one electron while preserving the large-N structure.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The electron-capture final state is obtained by ap- plying the appropriate destruction operators to this many-body coherent state, so that one proton and one electron are removed from the coherent domain while the large-N coherent structure is otherwise preserved.

prior_approach.content: Ref. [14] instead dynamically probed a simplified system of two-state oscillators coupled to a dissipative photon mode using weakly coupled external oscillators of variable frequency.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In Ref. [14] the excited states are not postulated through a Preparata-type variational form. causal_claim.content: A coherent state can make relevant energies exceed those of single incoherent particles when many particles participate.
causal_claim.evidence_span: If a suf- ficiently large number of such particles can enter a coherent state, the relevant energy scales need not be limited to those of single, incoherent particles.

causal_claim.content: The subsequent neutron can induce formation of deuterium, tritium, or transmuted isotopes through capture by nuclei.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The subsequent neutron can then be captured by a light or heavy nucleus, producing deuterium, tritium, or a transmuted isotope, depending on the material and on the nuclear channel involved.

causal_claim.content: Above a threshold density, the system lowers its energy by forming a collective state.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Above a density-dependent threshold, the system can lower its energy by forming a collective

causal_claim.content: Above a density threshold, the system forms a lower-energy collective coherent state.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Above a density-dependent threshold, the system can lower its energy by forming a collective state in which the proton oscillations are phase-correlated with a self-generated electromagnetic field.

causal_claim.content: The energy gap makes the coherent ground state thermally robust.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The coherent ground state is therefore separated from the incoherent perturbative ground state by an energy gap, which makes it robust against thermal fluctuations.

causal_claim.content: Slow neutrons from electron capture can be absorbed by nuclei, causing transmutations.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The slow neutrons produced by EC can be absorbed by heavy nuclei of the host metal, causing transmutations, or by light nuclei.

causal_claim.content: For deuterium loading, neutron capture can produce tritium.
causal_claim.evidence_span: For deuterium loading, neutron capture can lead to tritium formation.

causal_claim.evidence_span: This supports the basic physical assumption used in Ref. [30], namely that coherent excited states can exchange energy collectively at frequencies much higher than those of the individual oscillators

causal_claim.evidence_span: following the absorption of hydrogen in Ti, protons are bound to tetrahedral or octahedral sites in the Ti crystal structure, with an approximately harmonic potential.

causal_claim.content: Synchronization of proton wavefunctions causes condensation into a collective coherent state
causal_claim.evidence_span: The wavefunctions of the single protons become synchronized, through a complex mechanism analyzed in Refs. [1–3], and protons condense into a collective coherent state

causal_claim.content: Supplying suitable external power drives the system into a collective excited state

causal_claim.content: The neutron induces nuclear transmutation, increasing absorber mass and releasing gamma energy

mechanism_principle.content: Localized proton wavefunctions with very small overlap justify an approximate boson-like treatment of collective oscillations despite proton fermionic nature.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: However, the one-particle wavefunctions of protons bound to tetrahedral or octahedral sites in a metallic lattice are strongly localized, as shown in Ref. [3]. The overlap between wavefunctions centered at different sites is therefore very small, so that an approximate boson-like treatment can be used for the collective oscillatory degrees of freedom considered here.

mechanism_principle.content: In the proposed mechanism, the energy missing for electron capture is supplied by a collective excitation of the proton system.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: and the missing energy, approximately 0.78 MeV for particles initially at rest, is supplied by a collective excitation of the proton system.

mechanism_principle.content: Collective excitation energy can grow with the number of protons, exceeding single-oscillator spacings.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The basic idea is that collective excitation energies may scale with the number of participating protons, and can therefore be much larger than the level spacings of individual oscillators.

mechanism_principle.content: In the heavy-electron picture, proton oscillations indirectly increase effective electron mass by generating strong oscillating surface fields.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Proton oscillations were supposed to play only an indirect role, because they generated strong oscillating fields on the metal surface and these in turn increased the effective electron mass.

mechanism_principle.content: A small per-particle de-excitation in a large coherent domain can supply the full electron-capture threshold energy for one weak transition.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: If a coherence domain contains a very large number N of charged particles, a collective variation of the energy per particle of order ∆E/N can correspond to a macroscopic energy ∆E available for one weak transition.

mechanism_principle.content: The threshold is crossed not by accelerating one particle to MeV energies but by de-excitation of a many-body coherent state.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: In this sense the threshold mn −mp −me ≃0.782 MeV is not crossed by accelerating one proton or one electron to MeV energies, but by a small de-excitation of a many-body coherent state.

mechanism_principle.content: A small per-particle de-excitation of a many-body coherent state can supply the full weak-transition energy threshold, rather than accelerating a single particle to MeV energies.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: variation of the energy per particle of order ∆E/N can correspond to a macroscopic energy ∆E available for one weak transition. In this sense the threshold mn −mp −me ≃0.782 MeV is not crossed by accelerating one proton or one electron to MeV energies, but by a small de-excitation of a many-body coherent state.

mechanism_principle.content: Strong localization from the large proton mass justifies an approximate boson-like treatment without Pauli exclusion.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The bound eigenfunctions are strongly localized in the tetrahedral site wells, due to the large mass of protons. This justifies an approximated boson-like treatment without Pauli exclusion.

mechanism_principle.content: The coherent state is thermally robust because its energy gap is well above thermal energies
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: protons condense into a collective coherent state with an energy gap well above thermal energies, robust with respect to thermal fluctuations.

mechanism_principle.content: Finite-volume cavity behavior allows resonant modes in three dimensions
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The formation of resonant electromagnetic modes in all three space directions is possible because the finite volume acts as a natural cavity.

mechanism_principle.content: Mismatch between internal and external photon mode energy-momentum relations prevents internal modes from leaving the material, justifying the cavity effect
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: An external photon mode has a different ratio of energy and momentum. This mismatch prevents internal modes from propagating outside the material and thus provides a justification of the three-dimensional cavity effect.

mechanism_principle.content: Energy-momentum mismatch traps internal photon modes, justifying a 3D cavity effect
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: An external photon mode has a different ratio of energy and momentum. This mismatch prevents internal modes from propagating outside the material and thus provides a justification of the three-dimensional cavity effect.

mechanism_principle.content: Observed gamma signatures may be diluted because active coherent domains occupy only a small sample fraction
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: If, at a given time, only a small fraction of the material volume is occupied by active coherence domains, the corresponding signal would be strongly diluted and could be hidden by ordinary photoelectric, Compton, and nuclear absorption processes in the metal.

mechanism_principle.content: Energy exchange depends on level splitting or transition matrix element setting the timescale
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: one must also compute the level splitting, or equivalently the transition matrix element, because this determines whether energy exchange can occur on a physically relevant time scale

mechanism_principle.content: In the coherent-proton mechanism, missing energy comes from a real collective excitation of the medium
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the missing energy is supplied by a real collective excitation of the medium

mechanism_principle.content: Observable rates in both frameworks require spectral enhancement, either from nuclear resonance or coherent many-body transition weight
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: in both cases an observable rate requires a non-trivial spectral enhancement, either a nuclear resonance or a coherent many-body transition with sufficient spectral weight.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper proposes that coherent proton states form and can be excited in hydrogen-loaded metals as a key theoretical ingredient.

hypothesis_statement.content: The coherent proton state is proposed to act as a collective energy reservoir for electron capture rather than to enhance fusion.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Thus the role of the coherent proton state is not to enhance ordinary fusion, but to provide, at least in principle, a collective energy reservoir for electron capture.

hypothesis_statement.content: Gamma energy may be partially reabsorbed by collective proton or deuteron degrees of freedom.

problem_motivation.content: A satisfactory microscopic theory for the anomalous phenomena in hydride metals is still lacking; in particular, a complete theory of coherent electron capture must go beyond a stable coherent ground state to microscopically derive the excited coherent-state structure and spectrum from the proton–photon Hamiltonian, including their transition energies, transition probabilities/strengths, and weak-interaction matrix elements.
evidence_spans: A satisfactory microscopic theory of such phenomena is still lacking.
These issues require knowledge of the spectrum and transition probabilities of the excited coherent states, which remains one of the main open problems of the model.

A complete theory of coher- ent electron capture should therefore combine the microscopic derivation of the coherent ground state, the localized proton spectrum of Ref. [3], and a many-body calculation of the excited coherent states and of their weak-interaction matrix elements.
The central open problem is the structure of the excited coherent states.
However, electron capture requires not only a stable coherent ground state, but also excited coherent states with suitable transition energies and transition strengths.

problem_motivation.content: The core physical challenge is coherent energy conversion across strongly mismatched energy scales, and what must be computed is not merely the total energy stored in a coherence domain but the spectral weight by which the local weak operator couples the initial coherent state to neutron-plus-neutrino final states, including whether this response contains a coherent super-extensive contribution scaling with the number of participating protons.
evidence_spans: The relevant physical problem is therefore a form of coherent energy conversion between strongly mismatched energy scales.

the ultimate quantity to be computed is not only the total energy stored in a coherence domain, but the spectral weight with which the local weak operator couples the initial coherent state to final states containing a neutron and a neutrino.

prior_approach.content: Refs. [1,2] previously studied the formation of a coherent ground state for many protons bound at interstitial/tetrahedral sites in a cubic metal lattice, oscillating with a local electrostatic frequency and collective plasma oscillations, and coupled to cavity/confined electromagnetic modes in a finite resonant volume.
evidence_spans: The formation of the coherent ground state has been studied in Refs. [1, 2]. In that model, a large number N of protons are bound to interstitial sites of a cubic lattice and oscillate with a local frequency determined by the electrostatic potential of the site. The protons are also coupled to electromagnetic modes confined inside a finite region of the material.
In Refs. [1, 2], we considered a system with a large number N of protons bound in potential wells centered at tetrahedral sites x1, . . . , xN in a cubic metal lattice.

All protons oscillate with the same elastic frequency ω defined by the local electrostatic potential; in addition, they are subject to collective plasma oscillations with a frequency ωp which depends on the proton density and is of the same magnitude as ω.
The protons also interact with cavity photons, i.e. electromagnetic modes confined in a finite volume of size ∼λ3, where λ is the resonant photon wavelength, related to ω and ωp.
Graphical representation of the coherent electron-capture process investigated in Refs. [1–3].

prior_approach.content: Ref. [3] previously provided numerical calculations of the one-particle proton spectrum in the local electrostatic potential for a typical lattice.
evidence_spans: The one-particle energy spectrum of protons bound by the local electrostatic potential has been computed numerically in Ref. [3] for a typical lattice with unit spacing d = 0.25 nm and a frequency ℏω = 0.41 eV.

prior_approach.content: Ref. [14] previously used a simplified model of coherent harmonic qubits / two-state oscillators coupled to a dissipative photon mode and dynamically probed by weakly coupled external oscillators, providing numerical evidence that coherent low-frequency oscillators can mediate high-frequency energy transfer between external oscillators.
evidence_spans: More recently, Ref. [14] has provided numerical evidence, in a simplified model of coherent harmonic qubits, that high-frequency energy transfer between external oscillators can occur only when the intermediate low-frequency oscillators are in a coherent state.

In Ref. [14] the excited states are not postulated through a Preparata-type variational form. Instead, a simplified system of N two-state oscillators coupled to a dissipative photon mode is probed dynamically by weakly coupled external oscillators of variable frequency.

The numerical results of Ref. [14], although obtained in a simplified two-level model, point in the same physical direction by showing that high-frequency energy transfer can be mediated by a coherent system of low-frequency oscillators.

prior_approach.content: Widom and Larsen [4] previously proposed electron capture in condensed matter, hypothesizing that the missing energy comes from an electromagnetic-interaction-induced increase in effective electron mass in matter; they also proposed gamma-ray suppression mechanisms based on this heavy-electron hypothesis.
evidence_spans: The occurrence of EC in condensed matter has been previously suggested by Widom and Larsen [4].
the missing energy in case of initial particles at rest was hypothesized to come from the increase of the effective electron mass due to the electromagnetic electron interaction in matter.

Widom and Larsen defended their proposal also in other articles [19– 21] and described a possible suppression mechanism of the gamma rays which originate from transmutations of heavy elements and reactions such as p+n →D+γ and D+n → T +γ. This suppression mechanism is also based on the heavy-electron hypothesis.

prior_approach.content: Gamberale / Ref. [30] previously analyzed electron capture by coherent protons, giving the first explicit weak-interaction calculation of neutron production from coherent proton states, estimating neutron production rates once a coherent excitation above threshold is available, and including rate equations linking pumping to final energy output.
evidence_spans: The electron capture by coherent protons as proposed in this paper has been previ- ously analyzed by Gamberale [30].

This made it possible to address a question which is not treated in the present review of the coherence mechanism itself, namely the or- der of magnitude of the neutron production rate once a coherent excitation above the electron-capture threshold is available.
The work also includes rate equations relating the pumping process to the final energy output, which are clearly relevant to applications.
Ref. [30] gives the first explicit weak- interaction calculation of neutron production from coherent proton states

prior_approach.content: In Ref. [30], the coherent ground state was modeled with a collective mixing-angle parametrization fixed by energy minimization; excited states were represented by nearby states in the same variational class (a Preparata-type Ansatz) with slightly modified collective parameters such as mixing angle and collective momentum; the electron-capture final state was built by applying destruction operators to the many-body coherent state, removing one proton and one electron while preserving the large-N coherent structure.
evidence_spans: The coherent ground state is parametrized by a collective mixing angle, fixed by minimization of the energy. A coherent excited state is then represented by a nearby state in the same class, with slightly different values of the collective parameters, for example a modified mixing angle and a modified collective momentum.
In the calculation of Ref. [30], the excited states were described by a Preparata-type Ansatz.

The electron-capture final state is obtained by ap- plying the appropriate destruction operators to this many-body coherent state, so that one proton and one electron are removed from the coherent domain while the large-N coherent structure is otherwise preserved.

evidence_spans: Related issues appear in the spin–boson models studied by Hagelstein and Chaud- hary [13, 34], where a large two-level transition can become resonant with many quanta of a low-frequency oscillator through multiphoton Bloch–Siegert anticrossings.

mechanism_principle.content: Strong localization of bound proton wavefunctions in lattice sites—due to the large proton mass and resulting very small overlap between neighboring-site states—allows the collective proton oscillations to be treated approximately as bosonic, effectively bypassing Pauli-exclusion constraints for the relevant collective degrees of freedom.
evidence_spans: However, the one-particle wavefunctions of protons bound to tetrahedral or octahedral sites in a metallic lattice are strongly localized, as shown in Ref. [3]. The overlap between wavefunctions centered at different sites is therefore very small, so that an approximate boson-like treatment can be used for the collective oscillatory degrees of freedom considered here.
The bound eigenfunctions are strongly localized in the tetrahedral site wells, due to the large mass of protons. This justifies an approximated boson-like treatment without Pauli exclusion.

mechanism_principle.content: The proposed coherent-proton mechanism supplies the ~0.782 MeV electron-capture threshold not by accelerating a single proton or electron to MeV energies, but by a small per-particle de-excitation of a many-body coherent proton state: because collective excitation/de-excitation energy scales with the number of participating protons, a change of order ΔE/N per particle in a large coherent domain can provide a macroscopic energy ΔE for one weak transition.
evidence_spans: and the missing energy, approximately 0.78 MeV for particles initially at rest, is supplied by a collective excitation of the proton system.
The basic idea is that collective excitation energies may scale with the number of participating protons, and can therefore be much larger than the level spacings of individual oscillators.

If a coherence domain contains a very large number N of charged particles, a collective variation of the energy per particle of order ∆E/N can correspond to a macroscopic energy ∆E available for one weak transition.
In this sense the threshold mn −mp −me ≃0.782 MeV is not crossed by accelerating one proton or one electron to MeV energies, but by a small de-excitation of a many-body coherent state.
